title: Write a hard passage closer to speech
statement: To ease a hard passage written for learners, write it closer to how people talk, packing fewer idea units into each clause.
detail: The RAND Reading Study Group's 2002 report, in a reading course's digest of it, says it can simplify comprehension challenges if writers write the way they talk (p. 96), and the digest gives the reason: printed text packs more idea units into each clause than speech (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/reading-science/DIGEST-rand-mr1465-2002.qmd`, lines 351-353). The claim before it names the sentences that cause trouble: embedded, dense, ambiguous or ungrammatical ones. The digest offers it as a drafting heuristic for reducing syntactic load without stripping content knowledge.

evidence.quote: Thus, it can simplify comprehension challenges if writers write the way they talk.
Because printed text packs more idea units per clause than spoken language, comprehension can be eased by writing passages closer to how people actually talk.
This occurs when a sentence is embedded, dense, ambiguous, or ungrammatical.
Gives passage authors a concrete drafting heuristic for reducing syntactic load in G3/G5 texts without stripping content knowledge.

citations.ref: RAND Reading Study Group 2002, Reading for Understanding (MR-1465)
